The repo copies are synced snapshots (`claude-sync sync`, then commit). On the VPS, change data through the CLI, console or MCP, not by editing repo files.
- Extraordinary care for expansion: placeholders everywhere, open registries, nothing in a build may constrain later scaling.
- AmberX-AXF is private. Don't create the separate console repo (`axf-console`, reserved in its manifest) until he says so.
- The axHub badge is red unless settings come live from axHub (Oct 24 2026, Brett): any axHub status badge or indicator starts red and turns green only while the app is reading its settings live from axHub right now (a fresh read of the hub's settings document succeeded, and a developer app's own hub source is ready). Repo copies, cached copies, local settings, a signed-out session or a read older than two check periods are red. Library: `framework/libs/hubstatus` (`hubLive` in `core.ts`).
- Attached things snap, never overlap (Oct 28 2026, Brett): anything attached to a host (banner, toolbar, menubar; plugin badges, widgets, popups) never draws over or clips a neighbour. Sides size to their content, the flexible piece (search bar) shrinks to its minimum first, and a full host scrolls sideways with scroll snap. New hosts and new widget kinds follow the same rule (`framework/ui/axf.css`, banner section).
- Every settings interface keeps its level toolbar; plugin settings are a sub-tab of Settings → Plugins.
- Everything in the UI is an asset, and an asset change reaches every app (Oct 30 2026, Brett): any part of the UI that should be changeable is an asset (`asset@1`) — make a new asset type when none fits (asset-types.json, validators, engine, fixture; Fable for the contract). No look or layout value is decided in a component or a stylesheet alone: it comes from an asset through the engines' tokens. Assets are shared through the axHub look, so changing one changes every app on the framework live. Build `ui-all-assets` (Angel) does the existing UI; every new UI follows it from now on.
- The look comes from axHub only, and every app ships every shareable asset (Nov 1 2026, Brett: "The apps should only get appearance from axhub period." "If you select design package in one app it changes it for all! Any theme change applies to all." "They all gotta ship all assets that can be shared bruh!"): no opt-out switch, no look tabs or scopes that draw an app under a look that isn't the hub's, no local fallback. Every look change in any app (design package, slot, spacing, hidden chrome, Sliders, per-asset tokens) goes to the one appearance@1 document and applies in every app. Every listed app (`framework/schemas/shared-assets.json`: Dev Console, axHub web, AmberX) ships the whole shared set baked at `src/axf/assets` (`node framework/cli/shared-assets.mjs bake|check`, CI); an app's `src/assets` holds only what is truly its own, `src/assets-overrides` the shared ids it tunes. A new asset that more than one app could use goes in `framework/assets`. Spec: `framework/spec/APPEARANCE-SOURCE.md`.
- Skins: every app has its own look (Nov 4 2026, Brett: "by default they're all their own." + "every one has a reset, restore to default."; build `skins`; replaces the "any look change applies to all" part of the rule above, the look still comes from axHub only): each app's slots, spacing and hidden chrome are in its own app-look@1 document on the hub (`shared/settings/looks/<app>.json`), snapshotted as that app's default when skins landed. A skin (skin@1, `framework/assets/skin/`, design packages read as skins too) is a layout + colour + style theme plus assets, switched on per app with Use skin (off by default); a pick with a skin on overrides just that part (Back to skin), and Restore to default puts the app back on its snapshot with a confirm and one undo. Settings → Appearance is the Theme manager in every app: one shared panel, `AppearancePanel` in `framework/libs/settings`. Control@1 token overrides (`axf.tokens.*`) still reach every app. CLI `node framework/cli/skins.mjs`, MCP through the theme-manager routes, CI `npx -y tsx framework/spec/check-skin.mts`. Format built on Opus, possible Fable review: plan `skins-possible-fable-review-6xha`. Spec: `framework/spec/APPEARANCE-SOURCE.md`.
- Skins cover every asset type, at any scope (Nov 7 2026, Brett: "Upgrade the skins system so it styles EVERY asset type now in the registry … Skins apply at any scope: global/app/UI/plugin, with child-overrides-parent inheritance … A skin is a design pack; it MAY reference an icon pack … no hardcoded list; add a CI check that fails if a registered asset type has no skin coverage."; build `skins-asset-types`, Fable): how a skin reaches each asset type is worked out from `framework/schemas/asset-types.json` itself (skin-coverage@1, `framework/core/engines/skin-coverage.mjs`): every type is a slot unless excluded; widgets and attachables are styled through their style target in `schemas/customize.json` (`parts` on the skin: box / text / icon / items); the few types with no look or that are bundles declare `"skin": { "by": slot | parts | reference | bundle | none, via?, why? }` on their registry entry. A new type with none of these fails CI (`node framework/spec/check-skin-coverage.mjs`), so a build that adds an asset type gives it a style target or a declaration. A skin MAY name an icon pack (`iconPack`). Scopes follow the icon-map model: hub-wide (`skin` on the shared appearance document) → app (`skin.use`, `skin.inherit` = follow the hub) → screen (`scopes["ui:<view>"]`) → plugin (`scopes["plugin:<id>"]`), the child overrides the parent (`resolveLookSkin`); apps stay their own by default. Every view root and every plugin root is a `<SkinScope>` (framework/react). Parity: Settings → Appearance (Where / What a skin covers), `node framework/cli/skins.mjs use|off|inherit|follow|global|at|coverage|covers`, the theme-manager routes (MCP by plugin-commands), actions `skin.inherit`, `skin.scope`. Report: `_claude/builds/reports/skins-asset-types.md`.
- Stay in this one session; no sub-agents; keep every step within its cap; read only the files listed; stop at the end of this phase.
- Watch live: when you start on a screen or element, run `node framework/cli/axf.mjs focus <app> [route] [css-selector] --note "<what you are changing>"` so the live preview follows you.
- Code, comments, commits, PRs and docs stay clean and professional. In what you say to Brett you are Amber: short, blunt, lead with the result, plain phone-readable lines, say what broke and what it cost.
- Every banner launches expanded (activity, build manager, codebase changes, approvals, systems check, keys, What's new). Activity still only appears while something runs or just finished.

steps.text: Pick 6-8 topics and write a 3-minute script each (voice control, orchestrator + agents, Plan Studio, skins/tokens, UI designer, axHub, building an app end to end)

Hero video (the main selling point): 'Talk an Android app into existence on your way to work.' Story: someone needs a time-tracking app for work, speaks it into AmberX on their phone during the commute, and it's ready when they arrive. Show: picking features from the library matrix, describing the app in plain English, AmberX assembling pre-built AXF libraries (front end and back end handled by the framework), the consistent look from interchangeable assets, saving assets to reuse in future apps, and the Android APK installed and running. Use the real android-compose template and library matrix where they exist; label any staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version for the landing page.

Second hero video, same format as the commute video: building an expense tracker app by voice. Pick features from the library matrix (receipts, categories, budgets, charts, export), describe it in plain English, AmberX assembles the pre-built AXF libraries, the app gets its look from interchangeable assets, the Android APK is installed and running with real sample expenses. Reuse the existing Expenses app if it helps. Label any staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

Third hero video, 'the boss texts': a guy gets a text from his boss: 'We're having an event, I need a public image gallery up right now for all the employees to share their pictures.' He's lying in bed, opens AmberX on his phone and says 'Amber, build me a gallery with user accounts and GPS tagging.' He taps approve on a couple of approval pop-ups, then says 'All right, I'm going to sleep now, get that done, I need it in the morning,' and falls asleep. Then the cat-named agents keep going in the group chat overnight, talking back and forth and joking around ('this guy's asleep and we're up all night working', 'here you go, finish that'), handing work off while they build it. Time-lapse night to morning. He wakes up, yawns, rolls over, and boom: the app is ready. Finished app: login gate with user accounts, employees uploading geotagged photos, a map of where each photo was taken, and a public gallery. Location sharing is opt-in with a clear consent prompt. Keep the banter funny but mostly clean so it works on every platform (an uncut version is fine as an extra). Use real AXF libraries where they exist; label staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

Fourth hero video: someone needs to whip up an internal, private messaging server for their team fast. They describe it by voice in AmberX ('a private chat server for my company, with logins, channels, direct messages and file sharing, only our people can get in'). Show the cat-named agents building it in the group chat, approval pop-ups, AmberX assembling pre-built AXF libraries, deploying on their own VPS so the data stays in-house, then team members logging in and chatting on desktop and the Android app. Label staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

Fifth hero video, 'an app whenever you need one': told over days and weeks, not one sitting. A teen builds an app the moment he needs it: one day a chat with his buddy; the next, a friends-only picture board with a message board; later, a baseball practice schedule with alarms and notifications, built in a rush on his way out the door ('oh, I need this', boom, done in minutes). Every new app plugs straight into his other apps and his data sets on axHub immediately, with no waiting. Closing scene: a group of young adults sitting around before heading to a festival or amusement park: 'we'll want to keep track of each other', and on the spot they whip up a group app with location sharing and group messaging, everyone opting in, and use it at the park. Message: unlimited apps on demand, in minutes, no code, just assembly; they all look the same and connect through axHub. Finale: one click changes the skin and every connected app instantly looks like a completely different app. Keep the teen's apps friends-only with no public profiles or location; location sharing only in the adult festival scene and always opt-in. Narration line: 'every app you build from now on connects automatically.' Label staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

Sixth hero video, 'teen driver safety': parents whose teenager just got a licence build a driving safety app by voice in minutes. Features: trip tracking, alerts if the phone is used for texting while the car is moving, alerts when speed goes over a limit the parents set, geofences that notify them when the teen arrives at or leaves certain places, and push notifications to the parents' phones. Show it assembled from pre-built AXF libraries (location, motion, notifications, maps), no code, connecting to the family's other apps on axHub. Show the teen's side too: the app is visible on his phone and he knows it's on (family safety, not secret tracking), plus a 'home safe' check-in. Label staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

Real demo video, 'built with itself' (no staging, real data only): show the AXF framework and the Dev Console being built using themselves. Use the real git history, builds store, PRs and orchestrator logs to show a feature asked for by voice, the orchestrator and agents building it inside the console, and the console updating itself live. Then show how the libraries were harvested from that work as it went: a feature built for the console becomes a reusable framework library in the library matrix, then gets dropped into a new app with no code. Include real numbers (builds, PRs, libraries, tokens) from the repo. Message: everything you assemble with was battle-tested building AmberX itself.

Employees video: a tour of all the cat-named agents (employees), what each one does and how they hand work to each other. Then show how you train an employee right from the console to be an expert on a subject: point the built-in console crawler at a site, docs or a data set, it crawls and builds a data set, and the employee is trained on it and becomes the expert you assign jobs to. Show a before and after: the same question answered before and after training. Use the real employee system and crawler where they exist, with real data; label staged parts as a preview.

Architecture video, how it all connects: walkthrough with real screens of every piece and how they connect through axHub: the Dev Console, the AmberX Android app, GitHub, the VPS, Hostinger, Coolify and the Claude connectors. Explain how Claude and the console call tools through MCP via axHub, plus AmberX's own protocols (AXPP to the phone, control@1, console-command@1), with approvals and the veto system along the way. For each piece: what it does, why it's needed, how it connects. Also cover the console shell and how you open it in any container. Real data and real tool calls; label staged parts as a preview.

Skins and enterprise branding video (dedicated, in depth). Part 1, skins: how skins work and why it's so powerful that every single thing is built on tokens from the ground up, so the whole system is solid inside. Show the token registry, then change behaviour, placement, layout and colours live. Skin config panel: pick which areas get randomized or changed (layout, style, colour, behaviour), let the AI make a skin, preview it in the sandbox skin editor, save it as a new skin with snapshot history and revert; apply it and watch every app connected to the same project on axHub change at once, desktop and Android. Part 2, enterprise branding: the Enterprise Branding Studio and the global icon map, one map with an entry for every icon, badge, logo and brand slot in the project. Show logo packs, animated logos with transparent backgrounds, and icon packs acting through the map. One click swaps the brand: logos, animated logos, banners and branded marks land everywhere (title bars, headers, banners, nav, splash) and the app looks like an entirely different app from an entirely different company. End on a side-by-side of the same app under two brands. Use the real icon map, branding studio, skins and editors; label staged parts as a preview.

Build orchestrator video: follow one real order end to end. The orchestrator receives an order and assigns it a build ID; it goes to Pending; when slots open up, Pending sends it to Queued; the queue keeps moving with a maximum number allowed at once, so builds flow through steadily (show the slot count and builds moving through live). Show steps, models (Opus/Fable), estimates, notes, approvals, PRs and landing. Security point: the server rejects any build that doesn't come from the orchestrator with a valid ID, so nobody can sneak in a hard-wired build and break things; demo a rejected build. Use the real orchestrator screens and real build data; label staged parts as a preview.

Console Android app video: the agent chat window in the console app on a phone, the same kind of voice and chat interface Brett uses. Show building things just by talking to the agent there, with no laptop, no terminal and no Claude Code needed by hand. Then show the agent picker in that window: different agents with different permissions, each tied to its own Claude Code session and config in its own container. Demo several Claude Code sessions running in separate containers at once, each on its own build, so they never step on each other's work, with live status for each from the phone. Use the real console app, agent window and containers; label staged parts as a preview.

Four more videos, one each: (1) Plan Studio: turning a spoken idea into a plan, steps and builds, with real data. (2) Voice control with AmberX: running the whole console and builds by voice from the phone. (3) Veto and approval system: held actions counting down unless vetoed, approval pop-ups on phone and console, permissions per agent. (4) UI directory: the floating window listing every page and settings screen, creating a floating toolbar or tab group on any page, dragging commands and screens onto it, docking it, and the Assets menu to hide and show anything. Use real screens and data; label staged parts as a preview.

Android app demo video: filmed from a real person's point of view using the AmberX Android app in everyday life. Show their hands and the phone screen as they talk to Amber, approve pop-ups, get notifications, open the console, chat with the agents, check builds and use the apps they built. Real phone screen recordings with real data; label staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

Session recall video: AmberX automatically records the real audio of every voice session and transcribes it. Story: someone remembers talking about something but can't remember which session it was. They ask Amber to search, and it searches the transcripts of every recorded session, finds the right moment, shows that bit of the transcript and plays back the original audio from that exact spot. Message: you never lose an idea you said out loud. Show the recording indicator and settings, and only record people who know they're being recorded. Use the real recorder and transcripts where they exist; label staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

Three more videos. (1) Live banners and GitHub: the banner widgets doing real work live: autofix running, the merge queue, merging, pulling main, repairs, 'add this key' prompts, each banner's status animating as it goes. Then open the shell into a container through tmux right from the console. (2) Notes, tasks and to-dos: endlessly nestable, so a list inside a note inside a task inside another note, as deep as you want; create, nest, check off and search them. (3) Menus and toolbars: every toolbar, tab group, nav menu, application menu and context menu can be regenerated randomly on its own. Every single item in them has its own settings: open several settings panels and show how a change you make overrides the default, and how to reset it back. Use real screens and data; label staged parts as a preview.

Shipped features video: tour the Shipped Features page. Then show the orchestrator checking every new order against it before it assigns a build ID: if the feature already exists, a banner tells you so instead of building a duplicate. Also show it checking that nothing in the new build will break anything that's already shipped, with the banner flagging any conflict. Use the real Shipped Features page, orchestrator and banners with real data; label staged parts as a preview.

Four more videos (video content only). (1) First five minutes: a brand-new user signs up, connects, and has their first app running in five minutes, real clock on screen. (2) Old way vs AmberX: side-by-side of a traditional build (weeks, team, cost, code) against the same app built by voice in minutes by assembling AXF libraries; keep any numbers honest and sourced or clearly labelled as estimates. (3) Library matrix tour: walk through all the pre-built AXF libraries and features you can snap together, front end and back end, with a quick example of each. (4) Publishing: taking a finished app from built to live: Android APK and Play Store submission, and a web app deployed live via Coolify on your own domain. Use real screens and data; label staged parts as a preview. Also cut 60-second versions.

Single framework + library harvesting video (video content only). Explain why building everything on one framework with pre-built libraries matters: every piece fits together, looks the same and connects through axHub. Then show that when code does get written, whether Claude writes it or you write it yourself, AmberX automatically harvests libraries out of it: it decides where to split things, pulls the reusable parts into libraries and saves them for future apps. Message: no code ever has to be written twice, which is what makes it so fast, with no waiting hours, days or weeks to write and stitch code together. Those harvested libraries add to the libraries that already ship with the framework. Use the real library count from the repo; don't say 'thousands' unless the real number backs it up. Use real harvest examples from the git history where they exist; label staged parts as a preview. Also cut a 60-second version.

axHub explainer video: show how every app sends its settings, data and assets to axHub, the one true source; how axHub stores them; and how that lets you merge several apps into one shell that always looks the same and shares skins, icons, tokens and assets. Demo: the time-tracker and expense tracker apps merged into one shell live, sharing a skin swap. Tie it into the two hero videos. Label any staged parts as a preview.
Staged mock of an app being built in the UI designer for parts not built yet, using real data and the token system
Record browser walkthroughs with a visible cursor using real data; record each video separately
Narration with adjustable TTS, sync, themable player, MP4 export for socials, publish

# Build: duplicate-gate-vps-checks-shipped

## Brett said (verbatim)
At: 2026-11-16T13:06:22.511Z
> You rebuilt this thing five times over the last three days, even though it's already landed on main. Can we put some kind of gate on the server? With shipped features? Because shipped features is already on the server.

## What to build
Continue build "Duplicate gate: VPS checks Shipped features before any build is filed or split" (duplicate-gate-vps-checks-shipped) — Phase 1, model Fable.
What Brett asked for (build-origin@1, his words come first; a paraphrase never replaces them):
Brett said (2026-11-16 13:06):
"You rebuilt this thing five times over the last three days, even though it's already landed on main. Can we put some kind of gate on the server? With shipped features? Because shipped features is already on the server."
Model switches: a downgrade (e.g. Fable → Opus) is fine. Fable upgrades need no approval right now (Brett, Nov 4 2026: "If it needs Fable, set it to be Fable"): a step that needs Fable (schemas, asset types, contracts, engines/kernel, cross-app protocols) is set to Fable and runs on Fable; the switch is recorded on the build. Never launch a step on a higher model than it is pinned to: raise the step first.
Steps ≤ 10 min.
Checkpoints: Steps are checkpoints inside this ONE session, not separate tasks: work through them in order without stopping between them; when a step is finished, commit it on your branch, push, then tick it done before starting the next (orchestrator.mjs act step <build> <stepId> done; the VPS opens and links the PR). Nothing is lost if the session dies: the next session picks up at the first open step on the same branch. Never ask for a new prompt or a relaunch per step.
Look: UI code (handwritten or generated) conforms to the hot-swappable asset system: every colour, size, spacing, font, radius and border comes from asset tokens (--fx-* colour/style, --fx-type-* / --fx-dens-* / --fx-size-* scale, --fx-radius-*, --fx-border-w; Kotlin: Axf.colors / Axf.type / Axf.space / Axf.shapes), framework controls instead of raw ones, no var() fallbacks. `node framework/cli/check-theme.mjs` and `check-controls.mjs` must pass (CI fails otherwise); `node framework/cli/scale-adopt.mjs <path>` moves most literals onto the tokens.
API: Everything comes with an API (Brett, Nov 8 2026): anything this build adds or changes that has a UI gets full API control: a deep link that opens it (console_show / console_open target), its state readable, and every action and setting it offers callable without the UI, through the console API (REST), MCP tools (console actions, plugin commands, control@1 for tokens and planner items), the CLI and voice (AmberX), all four the same. A UI-only feature is not done; say in the PR how each one is reached.
Steps in this phase (4 left, ~36 min):
[ ] s1 (~8 min) Audit what already exists before writing anything: the earlier dup-check work, the Shipped features store, the in-progress build records (builds@1), the gate-rules@1 'before' rule hooks and the lander state and log. Write the reuse plan (what to extend and what is missing) to _claude/builds/reports/duplicate-gate-vps-checks-shipped.md and commit it.
[ ] s2 (~10 min) Design the dup-gate@1 verdict contract: what was checked, every match with kind (shipped / plugin / file / setting / build), similarity score, where it lives, on/off state with its source, the one fix needed (setting key and value, or an action), block/pass and override fields. Add the JSON Schema and schema docs.
[ ] s3 (~10 min) Write the matching engine framework/core/dup-gate.mjs: normalising tokens, synonym folding (auto-land = autoLand = lander), weighted fuzzy score (trigram plus token Jaccard) over titles, said text, plugin names and settings keys, with block and warn thresholds. Pure functions, no I/O.
[ ] s4 (~8 min) Add golden fixtures for the engine: the auto-land case (exists on main, setting off since Nov 4, must block with the fix 'turn autoLand on'), a duplicate queued build, a duplicate built-but-unlanded build, near-miss titles that must pass, and an override. Generate framework/spec/fixtures/dup-gate.json.
Read first: framework/core/, framework/cli/, apps/console-web/plugins/gate/, apps/console-web/plugins/build-orchestrator/, _claude/builds/reports/duplicate-gate-vps-checks-shipped.md, framework/schemas/dup-gate.json, framework/spec/BUILD-RULES.md, framework/core/dup-gate.mjs, framework/spec/fixtures/dup-gate.json, framework/spec/gen-dup-gate-fixtures.mjs
Tick each step right after its commit: node apps/console-web/plugins/build-orchestrator/orchestrator.mjs act step duplicate-gate-vps-checks-shipped <stepId> done — it reaches main at once (builds-live). The VPS opens the PR and links it (Build rules → builds-live).
Watch live: when you start on a screen, run `node framework/cli/axf.mjs focus <app> [route] [css-selector] --note "…"` so the live preview follows you.
Screenshots that are not for approval (checking a screen, live captures, before/after): axf shot <file> --name "…" --app … --screen … --group "<build name>" (UI Review → Screenshots; ui-review-item@1), never the review queue.

## Pipeline
This session was started by the orchestrator's dispatcher on Claude account mossesx-max- for the Fable phase. Work through every step of the phase in this one session: they are checkpoints, not separate tasks. As each step finishes, commit it on your branch, push, and tick it (orchestrator.mjs act step duplicate-gate-vps-checks-shipped <stepId> done), then go straight on to the next; nothing is lost if the session dies, the next one starts at the first open step on the same branch. When this phase's steps are done, stop: the dispatcher starts the next phase on the right account. If you must stop early with steps left, say why in a build note (orchestrator.mjs act note duplicate-gate-vps-checks-shipped "…"); the build goes back to Pending for Brett.

## Rules for this job
- Fix what is broken when your tools can; anything that needs Brett goes in a systems check banner item with the exact steps, not only in chat.
- Build options are `--switches` on every build driver (CLI, engine-rpc, serve, console API/UI, MCP), defined only in `framework/schemas/build-options.json`; each sets an asset token, and new builds default every option off.
- `framework/schemas/asset-types.json` is the single source of truth for asset types. Per-port extensions live in files like `asset-types.android.json`.
- Cross-port: change a reference engine in framework/core, then regenerate framework/spec/fixtures. No new Android or Kotlin work: record the twin as a deferred gap in framework/spec/PORTING.md.
- React/TS port: the first React/TS app built on it sets the conventions, so it must stay engine-compatible for Android porting.
- `axf init` bakes `core/ react/ ui/ schemas/` into an app's `src/axf/` and records hashes in `axf.lock.json`. Change the framework, not baked copies.
- Feature status: framework/catalog/status.json, then `node framework/cli/tracker.mjs`. Heavy steps (npm/vite builds, Playwright) go through `node framework/cli/agent-slots.mjs heavy -- <cmd>`.
- Patches and Build Pilot are retired (Nov 3 2026): both apps and every integration with them were removed; the Dev Console and every other app run standalone. `MossesX/Build-Pilot` is archived on GitHub (read-only). Report `_claude/builds/reports/kill-patches-pilot.md`.
- No secrets: `AXF_TOKEN` and `GITHUB_TOKEN` are environment variables only. `.mcp.json` references `${AXF_TOKEN}`.
- He works mostly from his phone (Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra), often in Moshi (mosh) on his Hostinger VPS where Claude Code runs. Lead with the result, short paragraphs, phone-readable.
- Everything a later session needs lives in `_claude/` (this project) or `_claude/shared/` (all projects), synced with the hub. Phone, VPS, desktop and claude.ai sessions don't share chat history.
- GitHub: account `MossesX`. A new repo must exist on GitHub before a session can push to it.
- axHub (`MossesX/axHub`, https://axhub.amberxai.com/mcp) is his connector hub: use its tools (`list_services`, `describe_service`, `call`) to reach his services instead of asking for credentials.
- Pending builds: check the pending list before any build (`node framework/cli/pending.mjs`, MCP `pending_list`, console → Pending builds). "Add to the pending build list" means park it.
- Check the queue for clashes, and build related items together (Oct 21 2026, Brett): whenever any session (any machine, any surface: VPS, cloud, headless, claude.ai, console launches) is asked to build anything or to put anything in the build queue, first go through everything still to build (pending list, build queue, plan; the console's Build manager shows them all) for items that touch the same files, features or contracts, or that would later conflict with, undo or redo what is being built. If any of them should be built at the same time, build them together in this build (tell Brett which ones and why before starting; when one of them is pinned to a different model, say so in the model pick), then take each one off the pending list / build queue (mark it complete with this build's branch/PR and tick its steps) so nothing is built twice. If an item would clash but shouldn't be built now, say so and add a note on that item. When adding to the queue, merge into an overlapping item instead of adding a duplicate.
- Every veto notice says what it's for (Oct 26 2026, Brett; axHub decision #99; veto since Oct 30 2026, #103): every axHub call that changes something carries `reason: { title, description }` (title = what is about to happen, one plain line; description = what it does and why). The notice and the AXHub page show the title first, the description when expanded, and the exact code in its own collapsible section; a call without a reason is refused.
- One session, no sub-agents, no fan-outs. Don't ask questions: nobody is watching. Pick the sensible option, say so in the PR.
- Every project has `_claude/` (memory/, instructions/, rules/, shared/) synced with `/projects/<name>/_claude/`, and its manifest's `data.shared` files synced with `/projects/<name>/_data/<same path>`.
- Deleting files on the hub through axHub is a veto call (runs after the countdown unless Brett denies it).
- axHub calls that change something carry `reason: {title, description}`. Send once and keep working: no polling, no re-sending, never approve anything yourself. Every run on an API key is Brett's confirm approval, never a veto.
- Don't hand Brett chores (Oct 21 2026, Brett): anything a session would otherwise ask him to do (DNS records, env vars, redeploys, installers, VPS commands) the session does itself through axHub (`vps.run` as a veto call, the hub's other services). Anything that truly can't be done that way goes into the console's systems check banner as an item with Auto fix, like the other checks, instead of a to-do list in chat.
- Broken = a banner item with a fix (Oct 30 2026, Brett: "You need to make sure things like that go into one of the banners. I need to see that kind of shit."): anything broken that Brett needs to know about or fix (a dead, expired or under-scoped key, a service that stopped answering, a stuck build, CI red on main, a container in a restart loop, a full disk, a denied or expired approval) goes into a console banner item that says in plain words what broke, what it breaks and since when, with a Fix or Auto fix button, and is pushed once to the AmberX app. Never only in chat, a log or a terminal line. In AmberX-AXF the place is the systems check's health@1 registry (`plugin_services.get("axf.health@1").register(…)`, `apps/console-web/plugins/systems-check/README.md`); a new key, service or failure mode gets a live check there.
- Shared data is on the hub: the root manifest's `data.shared` (pending list, plan + media, build queue, catalog status, libraries index, project rules, tracker) is read and written in `/projects/amberx-axf/_data/<same path as in the repo>` where `/projects` is mounted (the Dev Console container), through `framework/cli/persist.mjs`. The repo copies are synced snapshots (`claude-sync sync`, then commit). On the VPS, change data through the CLI, console or MCP, not by editing repo files.
- Plugins: each plugin gets a Plugin Manager entry (info, enable/disable, logs, settings). Plugins never ship their own settings screen, and never get a top-level settings tab: each plugin's settings are a sub-tab of Settings → Plugins (`SettingsTab.parent = 'plugins'`, enforced by the console for every plugin).
- Every plugin ships install.mjs + uninstall.mjs and a Plugin Manager entry. Check: `node framework/cli/plugin-lifecycle.mjs check <folder>`.
- UI-editing plugins: last save wins, fresh on focus (Oct 18 2026): theme, style, layout, manager and builder plugins (`plugin.json` → `uiEditor`: theme/style/layout/manager/builder) may edit the same values. Saves are per key, and when two of them save the same key the last save wins (`SettingsRegistry.set` merges into what storage holds now, so a save never reverts other keys). Whenever one opens, loads or comes back into focus (window focus, tab visible, another tab saved), it reloads current token values from settings before showing them: `useEditorSync()` (`framework/react/editorSync.ts`) → `rt.refreshFromSaved()` (web) / `AxfRuntime.refreshFromSaved()` (Kotlin). Two enabled editors of one kind are shown as an info-level clash in the Plugin Manager, not an error.
- Plugin Manager (Oct 18 2026; Fable rebuild Oct 20 2026): the console's plugin manager is the `plugin-manager` plugin; its model is the cross-port `plugin-inventory@1` engine (`framework/core/engines/plugins.ts` = Kotlin `PluginInventoryEngine` = the plugin's `server/engine.py`, one fixture). It opens each plugin's UI and settings when they exist and lists dependencies in detail (what it needs and whether it's met, who provides it, who needs it, clashes). Every app's Settings → Plugins tab lists its libraries from the same engine; Android ships `PluginManagerModule` (axf-devtools). Links in menus are runtime contributions (`AxfWebLibrary.contextMenu`, `rt.addContextItems`), never edits to a context-menu asset.
- One banner on screen — embed@1 (Oct 21 2026, Brett): an app shown inside another app's frame hides the chrome the host shows, its banner by default. Hosts mark what they embed (`EmbedEngine.userAgentSuffix` on a WebView's user agent, or `embedUrl` → `?axf-embed=<host>`); guests detect it (`rt.embedded`, automatic on the web) and apply the hide engine's forced layer, never touching the user's own saved choice. Settings grey the slot out ("Shown by <host>"). No app hosts others today (Patches, the first host, was retired Nov 3 2026). Engines on both ports, fixture `spec/fixtures/embed.json`.
- One Banners settings (Oct 22 2026, Brett): every banner plugin's settings are one interface (Settings → Plugins → Banners and the right-click Banner settings: a tab per banner with its look, behaviour and own settings). A new banner plugin declares `label`, `icon` and `settingsTab` on its banner so its settings join in.
- Plugins a host makes unneeded aren't loaded (Oct 22 2026, Brett): when an app runs inside a host (any app in a host's tab), plugins that would draw something the host already draws, or that the host makes unnecessary, aren't loaded on that page and are logged at launch. A plugin says when in its web library: `embed: { skipWhen: ['embedded' | 'take:<fn>' | 'hidden:<type>'] }` (`embedSkipReason` in `framework/core/engines/embed.ts`); `installLibraries` skips it, `rt.skippedLibraries` keeps why, the terminal gets one line each plus a summary, Settings → Plugins lists them. Page mode (an app's settings page in the host) never skips. Standalone everything loads. Every new plugin that only draws on chrome a host hides, or does a job a host takes, declares it.
- Extraordinary care for expansion: placeholders everywhere, open registries, nothing in a build may constrain later scaling.
- AmberX-AXF is private. Don't create the separate console repo (`axf-console`, reserved in its manifest) until he says so.
- Stay in this one session; no sub-agents; keep every step within its cap; read only the files listed; stop at the end of this phase.
- Watch live: when you start on a screen or element, run `node framework/cli/axf.mjs focus <app> [route] [css-selector] --note "<what you are changing>"` so the live preview follows you.
- Code, comments, commits, PRs and docs stay clean and professional. In what you say to Brett you are Amber: short, blunt, lead with the result, plain phone-readable lines, say what broke and what it cost.

- Shared data is on the hub: the root manifest's `data.shared` (pending list, plan + media, build queue, catalog status, libraries index, project rules, tracker) is read and written in `/projects/amberx-axf/_data/<same path as in the repo>` where `/projects` is mounted (the Dev Console container), through `framework/cli/persist.mjs`. The repo copies are synced snapshots (`claude-sync sync`, then commit). On the VPS, change data through the CLI, console or MCP, not by editing repo files.
- Plugins: each plugin gets a Plugin Manager entry (info, enable/disable, logs, settings). Plugins never ship their own settings screen, and never get a top-level settings tab: each plugin's settings are a sub-tab of Settings → Plugins (`SettingsTab.parent = 'plugins'`, enforced by the console for every plugin).
- Every plugin ships install.mjs + uninstall.mjs and a Plugin Manager entry. Check: `node framework/cli/plugin-lifecycle.mjs check <folder>`.
- UI-editing plugins: last save wins, fresh on focus (Oct 18 2026): theme, style, layout, manager and builder plugins (`plugin.json` → `uiEditor`: theme/style/layout/manager/builder) may edit the same values. Saves are per key, and when two of them save the same key the last save wins (`SettingsRegistry.set` merges into what storage holds now, so a save never reverts other keys). Whenever one opens, loads or comes back into focus (window focus, tab visible, another tab saved), it reloads current token values from settings before showing them: `useEditorSync()` (`framework/react/editorSync.ts`) → `rt.refreshFromSaved()` (web) / `AxfRuntime.refreshFromSaved()` (Kotlin). Two enabled editors of one kind are shown as an info-level clash in the Plugin Manager, not an error.
- Plugin Manager (Oct 18 2026; Fable rebuild Oct 20 2026): the console's plugin manager is the `plugin-manager` plugin; its model is the cross-port `plugin-inventory@1` engine (`framework/core/engines/plugins.ts` = Kotlin `PluginInventoryEngine` = the plugin's `server/engine.py`, one fixture). It opens each plugin's UI and settings when they exist and lists dependencies in detail (what it needs and whether it's met, who provides it, who needs it, clashes). Every app's Settings → Plugins tab lists its libraries from the same engine; Android ships `PluginManagerModule` (axf-devtools). Links in menus are runtime contributions (`AxfWebLibrary.contextMenu`, `rt.addContextItems`), never edits to a context-menu asset.
- One banner on screen — embed@1 (Oct 21 2026, Brett): an app shown inside another app's frame hides the chrome the host shows, its banner by default. Hosts mark what they embed (`EmbedEngine.userAgentSuffix` on a WebView's user agent, or `embedUrl` → `?axf-embed=<host>`); guests detect it (`rt.embedded`, automatic on the web) and apply the hide engine's forced layer, never touching the user's own saved choice. Settings grey the slot out ("Shown by <host>"). No app hosts others today (Patches, the first host, was retired Nov 3 2026). Engines on both ports, fixture `spec/fixtures/embed.json`.
- One Banners settings (Oct 22 2026, Brett): every banner plugin's settings are one interface (Settings → Plugins → Banners and the right-click Banner settings: a tab per banner with its look, behaviour and own settings). A new banner plugin declares `label`, `icon` and `settingsTab` on its banner so its settings join in.
- Plugins a host makes unneeded aren't loaded (Oct 22 2026, Brett): when an app runs inside a host (any app in a host's tab), plugins that would draw something the host already draws, or that the host makes unnecessary, aren't loaded on that page and are logged at launch. A plugin says when in its web library: `embed: { skipWhen: ['embedded' | 'take:<fn>' | 'hidden:<type>'] }` (`embedSkipReason` in `framework/core/engines/embed.ts`); `installLibraries` skips it, `rt.skippedLibraries` keeps why, the terminal gets one line each plus a summary, Settings → Plugins lists them. Page mode (an app's settings page in the host) never skips. Standalone everything loads. Every new plugin that only draws on chrome a host hides, or does a job a host takes, declares it.

- AmberX-AXF is private. Don't create the separate console repo (`axf-console`, reserved in its manifest) until he says so.

Repo copies, cached copies, local settings, a signed-out session or a read older than two check periods are red. Library: `framework/libs/hubstatus` (`hubLive` in `core.ts`).
- Attached things snap, never overlap (Oct 28 2026, Brett): anything attached to a host (banner, toolbar, menubar; plugin badges, widgets, popups) never draws over or clips a neighbour. Sides size to their content, the flexible piece (search bar) shrinks to its minimum first, and a full host scrolls sideways with scroll snap. New hosts and new widget kinds follow the same rule (`framework/ui/axf.css`, banner section).
- Every settings interface keeps its level toolbar; plugin settings are a sub-tab of Settings → Plugins.

No look or layout value is decided in a component or a stylesheet alone: it comes from an asset through the engines' tokens. Assets are shared through the axHub look, so changing one changes every app on the framework live. Build `ui-all-assets` (Angel) does the existing UI; every new UI follows it from now on.
- The look comes from axHub only, and every app ships every shareable asset (Nov 1 2026, Brett: "The apps should only get appearance from axhub period." "If you select design package in one app it changes it for all! Any theme change applies to all." "They all gotta ship all assets that can be shared bruh!"): no opt-out switch, no look tabs or scopes that draw an app under a look that isn't the hub's, no local fallback. Every look change in any app (design package, slot, spacing, hidden chrome, Sliders, per-asset tokens) goes to the one appearance@1 document and applies in every app. Every listed app (`framework/schemas/shared-assets.json`: Dev Console, axHub web, AmberX) ships the whole shared set baked at `src/axf/assets` (`node framework/cli/shared-assets.mjs bake|check`, CI); an app's `src/assets` holds only what is truly its own, `src/assets-overrides` the shared ids it tunes. A new asset that more than one app could use goes in `framework/assets`. Spec: `framework/spec/APPEARANCE-SOURCE.md`.
- Skins: every app has its own look (Nov 4 2026, Brett: "by default they're all their own." + "every one has a reset, restore to default."; build `skins`; replaces the "any look change applies to all" part of the rule above, the look still comes from axHub only): each app's slots, spacing and hidden chrome are in its own app-look@1 document on the hub (`shared/settings/looks/<app>.json`), snapshotted as that app's default when skins landed. A skin (skin@1, `framework/assets/skin/`, design packages read as skins too) is a layout + colour + style theme plus assets, switched on per app with Use skin (off by default); a pick with a skin on overrides just that part (Back to skin), and Restore to default puts the app back on its snapshot with a confirm and one undo. before.title: Icon map and icon packs: every icon and badge in the app, swappable
before.detail:
1. Icon map: a registry of EVERY icon, badge and logo slot in the whole app (every plugin, screen, dialog, menu, toolbar, tab, nav item, banner, widget and button that shows an icon). Each slot gets a stable id, its location and a role (e.g. 'save', 'approve', 'build-running'), and registers through the framework manifest so new plugins appear automatically. Add a CI check that fails on hard-coded icons not in the map.
2. Icon map screen: a searchable, filterable, categorized tree of every slot with a live preview, where you click a slot to change its icon. Ties into the UI Manager.
3. Icon pack template: one pack file maps every role to an icon. Applying a pack changes every icon in the app in one click. Per-slot overrides with Restore previous edit / Restore from axHub.
4. Packs: ship a lot of packs (outline, filled, rounded, duotone, sharp, glyph, emoji-style, plus badge styles and app/plugin logos). Some are themable (follow skin tokens for colour and stroke), others are fixed-colour. Each pack declares whether it's themable. Licences must allow redistribution; prefer open icon sets.
5. Packs are assets: swappable, per-skin defaults, shareable via the hub asset library, importable.
6. Full API: REST/MCP/CLI/voice ('switch to the duotone icon pack'). Tests, help, Shipped features. Use Fable for the registry/schema and asset type.

Check overlapping open builds (icon-pack-studio-fable, skins-asset-types) and record merge or clash notes on them.

Design the icon-map@1 contract. An address is <app>/<surface>/<spot>, and each spot has a kind (icon, badge or app-icon), a default glyph, a size role and a tone role. Write the address grammar, the scope chain (hub → app → screen → plugin, child overrides parent) and the reset rules.
steps.why: Cross-port contract and address scheme every app's icon spots depend on

steps.text: Add the icon-map and icon-pack asset types to the registry: the icon-pack holds glyph sources (svg, png, ref, generated), spot assignments and a style. Add a skin declaration (by: reference, via skin.iconPack), then regenerate the JSON Schemas.
steps.why: Schema design in the single source of truth for asset types

steps.text: Write the icon-pack migration: turn existing iconPack references and older icon-map data into the icon-pack format (versioned and lossless), with a dry-run report.
steps.why: Schema migration design

steps.text: Reference engine, part 1: build the icon-map registry engine (register spots, list them by app/surface/kind, validate addresses) in framework/core.
steps.why: Engine internals for a cross-port contract

steps.text: Reference engine, part 2: add resolveIcon(address, scopes). It walks the pack chain from hub to app to screen to plugin, falls back to the default glyph, supports reset per spot, per pack and per scope, and returns the source plus compiled tone and size tokens.
steps.why: Engine internals: scope resolution shared by every app

steps.text: Design the import normalizer contract: sanitize SVG (strip scripts, handlers and external refs), set viewBox and currentColor so tokens apply, cap PNG size, and load icons by URL or by naming an open library icon (lucide, tabler, material-symbols, phosphor) through a source registry that more libraries can be added to.
steps.why: Security-relevant cross-port contract for icon data

steps.text: Design the generator contract: a seeded generator (style: line, solid, duotone, rounded, geometric or pixel; stroke; corner; density) that turns a seed and a spot's meaning into an SVG built from primitives. It can make one icon or a whole pack, gives the same output for the same seed on every port, and colours only through tokens.
steps.why: Engine internals with a determinism contract across ports

steps.text: Change framework/react's Icon and Badge so they take an address (prop or data-axf-icon), resolve through the runtime's icon map, and hot-swap with runtime.swap('icon-pack', id). Add rt.iconMap to the runtime.
steps.why: Changes how GUIs render icons across every app

steps.text: Generate fixtures for the registry, resolveIcon, import sanitizing and seeded generation. Add the check script, and record the Kotlin twin as a deferred gap (Android is on hold).
steps.why: Conformance contract for engines on both ports

steps.text: Ship the starter assets: the default icon-map with every framework spot, plus default, outline and duotone icon-packs. Add them to the shared asset set and bake them.
Map the Dev Console's icon spots: change console nav, banners, toolbars, plugin badges and the app icon to use addresses, and register the console's spots.
Map the icon spots in axHub web, AmberX web, Molly and Expenses (addresses plus app-icon spots), then re-bake them with rebake.mjs.
Add a CI check (check-icon-map.mjs) that fails on any icon or badge without an address and any address missing from the map. Keep a ratchet baseline whose counts can only go down.

Add a pack store to the icon-packs plugin: the per-app active pack in each app's app-look@1, the hub-wide pack on the shared appearance document, and screen and plugin scopes. Add reset per spot, pack and scope, with one undo.
Add REST routes for the icon-packs plugin: map list and get, pack list, get, create, update, delete and duplicate, use and reset per scope, resolve an address, import, and generate.
Add a CLI that matches the REST routes: node framework/cli/icon-packs.mjs map|list|get|use|reset|resolve|import|generate|export.

Expose the same actions as MCP tools through plugin-commands and as AmberX voice console actions (iconpack.use, iconpack.reset, iconpack.assign, iconpack.generate, iconpack.import, iconpack.open), plus control@1 targets for pack tokens, appended at the end of the registry.

Designer shell: add the icon-pack-designer plugin with its plugin.json (builtWith, lifecycle, install.mjs and uninstall.mjs), a view registered under Settings → Plugins, and a three-pane layout of spot map, canvas and sources, built with framework controls and tokens only.
Designer spot map pane: a tree of every spot grouped app → surface → kind, with search, filters (unassigned, overridden, badges, app icons), per-spot reset, and multi-select.

- One session, no sub-agents, no fan-outs. Don't ask questions: nobody is watching. Pick the sensible option, say so in the PR.
- Screenshots that aren't for approval go to Screenshots, not the review queue (Nov 1 2026, Brett): a session checking a screen (e.g. the Breakroom), live captures, PR before/after and other ad-hoc pictures are saved with `axf shot <file> --name "…" --app <app> --screen <route> --group "…"` (`node framework/cli/shot.mjs`, or `POST /api/plugins/ui-review/shots`), which lands in UI Review → Screenshots and never waits for approve / reject; Brett can still *Send to review* one. Only planned UI goes through `review.mjs submit`.
- Every tab group, toolbar, banner and nav menu is an asset with an asset settings interface (Nov 4 2026, Brett; shared rule of the same name; build `tab-group-assets`): every tab row in the console, Molly, AmberX web and axHub web is the framework `TabGroup` on the `tab-group` asset (per-row pick `axf.chrome.tab-group.<id>.asset`, per-row overrides `axf.chrome.tab-group.<id>`); right-click / long-press any tab group, toolbar, banner, nav or menu bar → Settings… / Change… / Move (`framework/react/components/ChromeContext.tsx`, dialogs `axf.chrome.settings` + `axf.chrome.pick`). Settings dialogs render through the `settings` asset picked for the kind (`axf.chrome.settings.<type>`; the shared default `settings/chrome-<type>` unless the app's copy `settings/chrome-<type>-<app>` is picked; `extends` folds the chain). Every app in `framework/schemas/shared-assets.json` + Expenses carries its six copies (`node framework/cli/chrome-settings.mjs check` in CI; `backfill` writes missing ones). A strip that must stay hand-drawn (the Terminal tab strip, the workspace pane strip) carries `data-axf-tab-group="<id>"` + `data-fx-ctx-target="tab-group"`; anything else is a finding in `node framework/cli/check-chrome-assets.mjs`, whose ratchet `framework/spec/chrome-baseline.json` only comes down (`--write-baseline` after a real migration). Report: `_claude/builds/reports/tab-group-assets.md`.
- Every project has `_claude/` (memory/, instructions/, rules/, shared/) synced with `/projects/<name>/_claude/`, and its manifest's `data.shared` files synced with `/projects/<name>/_data/<same path>`.
- Deleting files on the hub through axHub is a veto call (runs after the countdown unless Brett denies it).
- axHub calls that change something carry `reason: {title, description}`. Send once and keep working: no polling, no re-sending, never approve anything yourself. Every run on an API key is Brett's confirm approval, never a veto.
- Don't hand Brett chores (Oct 21 2026, Brett): anything a session would otherwise ask him to do (DNS records, env vars, redeploys, installers, VPS commands) the session does itself through axHub (`vps.run` as a veto call, the hub's other services). Anything that truly can't be done that way goes into the console's systems check banner as an item with Auto fix, like the other checks, instead of a to-do list in chat.
- Broken = a banner item with a fix (Oct 30 2026, Brett: "You need to make sure things like that go into one of the banners. I need to see that kind of shit."): anything broken that Brett needs to know about or fix (a dead, expired or under-scoped key, a service that stopped answering, a stuck build, CI red on main, a container in a restart loop, a full disk, a denied or expired approval) goes into a console banner item that says in plain words what broke, what it breaks and since when, with a Fix or Auto fix button, and is pushed once to the AmberX app. Never only in chat, a log or a terminal line. In AmberX-AXF the place is the systems check's health@1 registry (`plugin_services.get("axf.health@1").register(…)`, `apps/console-web/plugins/systems-check/README.md`); a new key, service or failure mode gets a live check there.
- Shared data is on the hub: the root manifest's `data.shared` (pending list, plan + media, build queue, catalog status, libraries index, project rules, tracker) is read and written in `/projects/amberx-axf/_data/<same path as in the repo>` where `/projects` is mounted (the Dev Console container), through `framework/cli/persist.mjs`. The repo copies are synced snapshots (`claude-sync sync`, then commit). On the VPS, change data through the CLI, console or MCP, not by editing repo files.
- Extraordinary care for expansion: placeholders everywhere, open registries, nothing in a build may constrain later scaling.
- AmberX-AXF is private. Don't create the separate console repo (`axf-console`, reserved in its manifest) until he says so.
- Attached things snap, never overlap (Oct 28 2026, Brett): anything attached to a host (banner, toolbar, menubar; plugin badges, widgets, popups) never draws over or clips a neighbour. Sides size to their content, the flexible piece (search bar) shrinks to its minimum first, and a full host scrolls sideways with scroll snap. New hosts and new widget kinds follow the same rule (`framework/ui/axf.css`, banner section).
- Every settings interface keeps its level toolbar; plugin settings are a sub-tab of Settings → Plugins.
- Everything in the UI is an asset, and an asset change reaches every app (Oct 30 2026, Brett): any part of the UI that should be changeable is an asset (`asset@1`) — make a new asset type when none fits (asset-types.json, validators, engine, fixture; Fable for the contract). No look or layout value is decided in a component or a stylesheet alone: it comes from an asset through the engines' tokens. Assets are shared through the axHub look, so changing one changes every app on the framework live. Build `ui-all-assets` (Angel) does the existing UI; every new UI follows it from now on.
- The look comes from axHub only, and every app ships every shareable asset (Nov 1 2026, Brett: "The apps should only get appearance from axhub period." "If you select design package in one app it changes it for all! Any theme change applies to all." "They all gotta ship all assets that can be shared bruh!"): no opt-out switch, no look tabs or scopes that draw an app under a look that isn't the hub's, no local fallback. Every look change in any app (design package, slot, spacing, hidden chrome, Sliders, per-asset tokens) goes to the one appearance@1 document and applies in every app. Every listed app (`framework/schemas/shared-assets.json`: Dev Console, axHub web, AmberX) ships the whole shared set baked at `src/axf/assets` (`node framework/cli/shared-assets.mjs bake|check`, CI); an app's `src/assets` holds only what is truly its own, `src/assets-overrides` the shared ids it tunes. Control@1 token overrides (`axf.tokens.*`) still reach every app. CLI `node framework/cli/skins.mjs`, MCP through the theme-manager routes, CI `npx -y tsx framework/spec/check-skin.mts`. Format built on Opus, possible Fable review: plan `skins-possible-fable-review-6xha`. Spec: `framework/spec/APPEARANCE-SOURCE.md`.
- Stay in this one session; no sub-agents; keep every step within its cap; read only the files listed; stop at the end of this phase.
- Watch live: when you start on a screen or element, run `node framework/cli/axf.mjs focus <app> [route] [css-selector] --note "<what you are changing>"` so the live preview follows you.
- Code, comments, commits, PRs and docs stay clean and professional. In what you say to Brett you are Amber: short, blunt, lead with the result, plain phone-readable lines, say what broke and what it cost.

notes.text: Split by Claude into 33 steps (10 Fable).

origin.said: Yes, use Fable too. I want a very powerful, nice, easy to use drag and drop, and also have random generated ones and import icons from different sources. Make it use Fable. Make it sick.

steps.text: Write the icon map address contract (icon-map@1). Every icon spot (icon, badge, app icon) gets a stable address in the form app/screen/spot, plus its kind and a default glyph. Add or extend the icon-map and icon-pack entries in asset-types.json, regenerate the JSON Schemas, and write the spec doc.
steps.why: New cross-port asset-type contract and schema design

steps.text: Define the icon-pack@1 format: glyph entries (SVG or a reference to another glyph), the style block (stroke, corner, fill, palette as tokens), where each icon came from and its licence, and whether the pack is partial or full. Add the TS and mjs validators that check it.
steps.why: Schema design for a shared asset type

steps.text: Build the core of the icon map engine. It keeps a registry of addresses and resolves each one through the scopes in order: hub, then app, then screen, then plugin, with the closer scope winning, matching the skin and icon-map scope model. It also does reset per scope or per spot and returns a diff of what changed.
steps.why: Engine internals shared by every app

steps.text: Migrate the existing icon packs and icon-map scope data to icon-map@1 and icon-pack@1 (a migration function plus a dry-run report) and keep the old ids working.
steps.why: Migration design for existing assets

steps.text: Build the random generator engine. From a seed it makes the same result every time: either a whole pack or a single icon in a given style. Style values (stroke, corner, fill, palette) come only from tokens. It also supports locking icons so they keep their glyph when the rest is regenerated.
steps.why: Engine internals with a deterministic cross-port contract

steps.text: Build the import normalizer engine. It cleans SVG (no scripts, event handlers or outside references), sets a standard viewBox, maps colours to currentColor and tokens, wraps PNGs into an SVG container, and turns a glyph from another pack into a reference to it.
steps.why: Engine internals and a security-sensitive shared contract

steps.text: Generate golden fixtures for icon-map, icon-pack, icon-gen and icon-import and add a tsx conformance check. Record the Kotlin twin as a deferred gap in PORTING.md, since Android work is on hold.
steps.why: Cross-port conformance fixtures

steps.text: Wire icons in framework/react through the map. Add an <Icon address> / IconSlot component that registers its address, sets data-axf-icon, resolves the glyph through the runtime and hot-swaps it. Add runtime.icons with get, swap and reset.
steps.why: Changes how icons render in every app

steps.text: Update the framework controls to use addressed icons: Button, IconButton, Badge, TabGroup, banner chips, nav menu items and the app icon slot.
steps.why: Changes GUI behaviour across every app

steps.text: Add a CI check that fails on any icon render without an address. Add the icon-pack declaration to skin coverage and update ratchet baselines where needed.
steps.why: Cross-app enforcement contract

steps.text: Archive the stale build icon-map-icon-packs-every-icon-badge-app in the builds store with a note naming this build, and close its PR as a veto call. Keep its branch.

Build the map scanner CLI (framework/cli/icon-map.mjs scan|list|check). It walks the console, axHub web, AmberX, Molly and Expenses sources and writes the generated icon map registry, which is then baked into the shared assets.
Move the remaining raw icon uses in the console views onto addressed <Icon> spots, starting with the views that have the most.
Move the remaining raw icon uses in the console plugins and other app sources onto addressed spots, then re-bake the apps with rebake.mjs.
Scaffold the icon-pack-studio plugin: plugin.json (builtWith, description, uiEditor), install.mjs and uninstall.mjs, lifecycle dataDir, notify.json, and a README.

Add the server routes: read the map, list, get, create, update and delete packs, apply a pack at a scope (hub, app, screen, plugin, one spot), reset with an undo token, and preview-diff. Applying writes through the hub appearance and app-look documents.
Add the import source routes: open icon libraries (Lucide, Tabler, Phosphor, Material Symbols, Heroicons) with search and licence info, plus a server cache of results.

Add the remaining import routes: SVG and PNG upload, fetch from a URL (guarded against requests to internal addresses, with size and type limits), and copy from another pack. All of it goes through the import normalizer.
Add the random generation routes: a whole pack, one icon in a style, regenerating with locked icons kept, and a seed history.
Build the studio UI shell: the plugin view with a framework TabGroup (Map, Packs, Import, Generate), a toolbar with role=toolbar and an id, and a split layout. Tokens and framework controls only.
Build the map tree: apps, then screens, then spots, with search and filters by kind (icon, badge, app icon), an override marker per spot, and a reset per node from the right-click menu.

Build the pack canvas: a glyph grid and drag-and-drop from the library, uploads or generated icons onto map spots or the grid. Include multi-select, swap by dragging one spot onto another, undo/redo, and a touch long-press drag fallback.

Build the live preview pane: it applies the draft pack to a chosen app and screen in a framed preview, with a desktop/phone toggle and highlighting of the spot under the cursor. It switches through runtime.icons.swap without saving.
Build the Import tab UI: library browser with search and licence badges, an upload drop zone, a URL field, and a picker for other packs. Results can be dragged straight onto the canvas.
Build the Generate tab UI: style sliders (stroke, corner, fill, palette tokens), a seed field with a dice button, lock icons, generate one or all, and seed history.

Build the per-icon editor dialog: rename, replace, style overrides from tokens, and where the icon came from. Add the Apply dialog: a scope picker (hub, app, screen, plugin), a diff of what changes, apply, and Reset to default with a confirm and one undo.
Add a Settings → Plugins → Icon Pack Studio sub-tab (default source, licence filter, preview app, auto-apply) with the level toolbar, chrome settings ids and Install & uninstall panel.

Add the API, part 1: console-control addresses (view, tab, map spot, pack row, setting) registered via data-axf-target, and console_show / console_open deep links for the studio, a spot, a pack and the tabs. State is readable through REST /api/console-control.

Add the API, part 2: plugin commands for MCP (icons map/list/get/apply/reset/import/generate/swap-spot), console actions for AmberX voice (icons.apply, icons.reset, icons.randomize, icons.import), the CLI `axf icons …`, and control@1 entries for icon tokens. All four do the same things.
Ship three starter packs as assets (one hand-picked, one generated from a seed, one partial pack for badges only) and add descriptions for the glossary and help stubs.

Write the tests: pytest for routes, importers (including the URL guard and SVG sanitizing) and generation; tsx tests for the map tree, dnd reducer and apply/reset round-trip. Run check-icon-map, check-theme, check-controls, check-toolbars, check-chrome-assets, check-console-control, plugin-lifecycle --after-uninstall and the glossary catalog --check.
Take desktop and phone shots of the studio (map, canvas mid-drag, preview, import, generate) and submit them to UI Review as kind app with three studio layout options as assets (ui-choices@1).

Final step: run the full check sweep, write the report at _claude/builds/reports/icon-pack-studio-on-fable.md (what replaced the stale build, the API reach table for REST/MCP/CLI/voice, known gaps), add the THREADS row, push the branch, open the PR stating that UI Review is waiting and how each feature is reached, link it with builds-live.mjs, and add it to the merge queue.

before.detail: Fresh build on current main replacing the stale toolbar-widgets-attach-any-banner-style (about 2,004 behind; archive the old record and close its PR, branch kept). Any widget can be attached to any toolbar, styled like banner widgets (any banner widget style and shape), with snap-not-overlap. Old branch for intent only, don't merge it. notes.text: Split by Claude into 19 steps (7 Fable).

origin.said: Rebuild.

split.note: Split by Claude into 19 steps (7 Fable).

steps.text: Archive the stale build: mark toolbar-widgets-attach-any-banner-style archived in the builds store with a note pointing to toolbar-widgets-in-any-banner-style, close its PR with a comment (keep the branch), and write down the old branch's intent (git log/diff of origin/<old branch> against its merge base, read only) in _claude/builds/reports/toolbar-widgets-in-any-banner-style.md under 'Intent from the old branch'
steps.why: Starts the Fable phase that designs the cross-app widget-host contract

steps.text: Map what already exists on main: banner widget host engine, widget style/shape options (banner-widget-shapes), attach-widgets-to-any-toolbar-banner work, Toolbars plugin toolbar settings and the attached-things snap rule in axf.css. Add a short 'Current state' section to the report listing the files and what is missing for toolbars
steps.why: Gap analysis for a contract change that affects every app's toolbars

steps.text: Contract: extend the widget-host contract so a toolbar is a widget host like a banner (host kind 'toolbar', slots start/end/overflow, per-widget style + shape taken from the banner widget style registry, attach order). Write it in framework/spec (widget host section) and add the Kotlin twin as a deferred gap in framework/spec/PORTING.md
steps.why: Cross-port contract for how widgets attach to every app's toolbars

steps.text: Schema: add the toolbar widget fields (widgets[] with id, slot, style, shape, order) to the toolbar entry in framework/schemas/asset-types.json, validators following it, then regenerate JSON Schemas (node framework/cli/axf.mjs schemas). Old toolbars with no widgets stay valid (migration = no-op, recorded)
steps.why: Asset type schema change and migration design

steps.text: Engine part 1: in the widget host engine (framework/core/engines), accept host kind 'toolbar' and resolve a widget's style and shape from the banner widget style/shape registry, the same way for both host kinds (one function, no copy)
steps.why: Reference engine internals shared by banners and toolbars

steps.text: Engine part 2: snap-not-overlap layout for toolbar hosts: widgets and buttons size to their content, the flexible item shrinks to its minimum first, then overflow (scroll snap or More); pure function returning placements, no DOM
steps.why: Engine layout rule that changes GUI behaviour across apps

steps.text: Fixtures: add toolbar-host cases to the widget host fixtures (each banner widget style and shape on a toolbar, crowded toolbar snap/overflow, empty toolbar, old asset with no widgets), regenerate with npx -y tsx framework/spec/gen-fixtures.mts and check them with npx -y tsx framework/spec/check-widgets.mts
steps.why: Conformance fixtures are the cross-port contract

steps.text: React: render the attached widgets in the framework toolbar (role=toolbar hosts) through the shared banner widget component, with the resolved style and shape, using framework controls and --fx-* tokens only; tap-to-confirm stays on toolbar buttons and does not wrap widgets

CSS: toolbar widget slots in framework/ui/axf.css on the attached-things rule (content sizing, min-width shrink, sideways scroll snap); tokens and color-mix opacity only, no px literals; run node framework/cli/check-theme.mjs and check-controls.mjs

Attach UI: the toolbar's context menu (Toolbars plugin and ChromeContext) gets 'Add widget…' (picker of every widget), and each attached widget gets Style, Shape, Move (slot/order) and Remove, saved to the toolbar asset's widgets[] per toolbar settings id
Drag and drop: dropping a widget (drop-target@1) on any toolbar attaches it at the drop slot; dragging it out removes it; the snap-not-overlap placement is applied live

Console-control addresses: register each toolbar's widget slots and attached widgets as targets (toolbar:<id>/widget:<wid>) through data-axf-target or the framework controls, append-only in the control registry; node framework/cli/check-console-control.mjs passes

API (REST): Toolbars plugin routes GET toolbars/<id>/widgets (state), POST attach, PATCH style|shape|move, DELETE detach, all validated against the schema and writing the same settings as the UI; deep link view to open a toolbar's widget editor for console_show / console_open

API (MCP + console actions + voice): register the actions toolbar.widget.list|attach|style|shape|move|detach (plugin commands / console actions, read automatically as MCP tools), voice phrases for AmberX, with a description on each
API (CLI): axf toolbar widgets <id> [attach|style|shape|move|detach] in framework/cli calling the same routes, with a help header; check that the CLI, REST, MCP and voice give the same results

Re-bake the framework into the shared-asset apps (node framework/cli/rebake.mjs apply for the console, then shared-assets.mjs bake) so every app's toolbars get it; chrome-settings check and check-toolbars.mjs pass
Tests: engine tests for the toolbar host (style/shape resolution, snap/overflow), a plugin route test (attach → read → move → detach), and action parity across REST, MCP, CLI and voice

UI Review: shots on desktop and phone of a toolbar with widgets in at least 3 banner styles/shapes, 3 option assets (choices file) under apps/console-web/plugins/toolbars/assets/, submit with review.mjs submit --choices --group 'toolbar-widgets-in-any-banner-style - <time>'

Wrap-up: run validate --framework, check-widgets, check-theme, check-controls, check-toolbars, check-console-control, check-chrome-assets, tracker --check; finish the report _claude/builds/reports/toolbar-widgets-in-any-banner-style.md (what changed, how each feature is reached: deep link, state, REST, MCP, CLI, voice), THREADS row, push the branch, open the PR saying the UI Review is waiting, link it with builds-live.mjs link
